newsitem.title: albania: Albanian protests spread beyond capital.
newsitem.headline: Albanian protests spread beyond capital.

text.p: Protests against Albania's crumbling network of get-rich-quick pyramid investment schemes spread beyond Tirana on Thursday to the western city of Vlore and Shkoder in the north, state media reported.

A strong police presence in the Albanian capital itself was intended to prevent a repeat of clashes on Wednesday when thousands of angry savers took to the streets to demand money back from Sude, once one of the most popular of the schemes.
Police were stationed in and around the city's main Skanderbeg Square, scene of anti-government demonstrations last year, and at key road junctions, eyewitnesses said.

But in Vlore, 150 km (90 miles) west of Tirana, protesters hurled stones at the city hall in fury that a local firm called Gjallica had postponed ressuming payments to depositors, Radio Tirana reported.
Two policemen were slightly hurt in the scuffles.
"People headed to the city hall. They shouted slogans against the government and threw stones and other objects which damaged the building," the radio said.
State television painted a similar picture in the northern city of Shkoder, where it described the atmosphere as "tense".

President Sali Berisha's conservative Democratic Party bore some of the the brunt of disappointed investors' ire in Tirana, where Sude's bankruptcy has left thousands out of pocket in Europe's poorest country.
The schemes, which seduced impoverished Albanians into selling everything they owned with promises of big returns on small outlays, mushroomed after the fall of communism in 1990.

"We are asking for our rights and for our money," said a middle-aged woman, one of a small crowd that returned for a second day to the western Tirana home of Maksude Kadema, a 30-year-old Romany gypsy better known by the diminutive "Sude'.
Police detained Kadema and 19 other people shortly after midnight on Thursday. They have been subsequently been charged with embezzlement, Tirana prosecutor Adnan Xhelili said.
Popular unrest in Albania's cities has coincided with a call for mass protests from the opposition Socialists, reformed heirs to the once dominating communists.

Demonstrators and some newspapers echoed the sentiment. In a commentary, the independent daily newspaper Koha Jone said the moment had come to mirror unrest in fellow Balkan states Serbia and Bulgaria.

"One would have thought the opposition would have learned a valuable lesson from the demonstrations in Belgrade and Sofia...but Berisha has learned more. Police violence has shown he will protect the squares with fanaticism," the paper added.

Local media reported that more than a dozen protesters were hurt in Wednesday's clashes and there were 29 arrests. Thousands of people took to the streets in Tirana and breakaway groups hurled stones at riot police armed with batons.
The collapse of Sude's scheme followed the demise of a similar company late last year. Four others have suspended repayments to investors.
The International Monetary Fund and the World Bank have both expressed concern at the spread of the shemes but the government has been slow to act against them.
